activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Airliner cabins are pressurized, but under regulations the cabin air pressure may be as low as it would be at 8,000 feet (about 2,400 meters) above sea level.
story:
Beatrice had never been on a plane before, and she was determined not to waste a single minute of the family trip worrying about it. Still, at the beach the day before departure, she sat on the sand with Juliet and Jaxton and admitted the truth. "There's one thing bugging me. My ears. I get ear pain, like, chronic ear pain. The doctor says it's a thing with me. And everyone says planes wreck your ears."

"That's pressure," Jaxton said, squinting at the waves. "Planes go high. High means pressure stuff."

"Then I'll bring snacks," Beatrice said. "My mom swears by gum, but if I can't fix the pressure, at least I can eat my feelings." She held up a paperback bag of chips she'd bought at the snack shack, still sealed and flat as a pancake. She was going to save it for the flight.

Juliet laughed. "You and your chips. Remember the science fair, when your volcano exposed the whole gym ceiling to baking soda foam?" That was last spring, and Beatrice still blushed a little thinking about it, but she had also won second place, because she'd been the only one to test three different ratios instead of guessing.

The next morning, halfway through the flight, her ears did ache, sharp and mean. She chewed gum until her jaw was tired. But then something else caught her eye. The chip bag in the seat pocket had blown up like a balloon, tight and shiny, as if someone had pumped it full of air. She turned it over in her hands. Nothing had opened it. Nothing had touched it.

Beatrice frowned and worked it out the way she'd worked out the volcano, step by step. The bag was sealed at home, down at sea level, near the beach. So the air inside matched the air outside then. Up here, the air outside the bag must be thinner than the air inside. She asked the flight attendant, "Is the cabin pressurized?" The attendant nodded. "It is, but under the regulations the cabin air pressure may be as low as it would be at 8,000 feet, about 2,400 meters, above sea level." Beatrice did the math in her head. That was higher than some mountains, and she was sitting in a chair eating pretzels.

When they landed and drove the last stretch to the coast, she pulled out a notebook and wrote it all down for Juliet and Jaxton, ending with a drawing of the bloated bag. Her ears still throbbed a little, and she'd tell her mom to ask the doctor about it before the flight home. But at the shoreline, where the plane seemed a world away, she opened the chips, now soft and ordinary again, and held the bag out to her little brother.

"Want some?" she said. "These have been to 8,000 feet."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During China's Qingming Festival, usually on April 4 or 5, families visit their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings.
story:
Alexander had been staring at the thin broom leaning in the corner of Room 214 for two days before he said anything about it. His grandmother had passed away that morning, frail and quiet at the end, and the nurses had let the family stay past visiting hours to say goodbye. His parents were still whispering by the bed, so Alexander wandered over and picked the broom up. It was old, with a worn wooden handle, and it had come from her house; he'd seen it in her kitchen closet a hundred times. But why had someone brought it here?

"You look like a defendant waiting for a verdict, standing there holding evidence," said Antoine, who had come with his mom after school. Anayah was right behind him, out of breath.

"It's her grave-sweeping broom," Anayah said quietly. "My family has one too. She told me about it in January, when I visited her with my grandmother." She pointed at the calendar on the wall, the one the nurses used for medication times. "Tomorrow is April fifth. Qingming. It usually falls on April fourth or fifth, and families visit their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings. She was planning to go to your great-grandfather's grave. She was going to teach Alexander how."

Alexander turned that over. So the broom hadn't wandered to the hospital by accident. Someone, probably his grandmother herself, had packed it before she came, even though she could barely lift a teacup. He tried to deduce when: not last week, because she'd been too weak. It must have been in January, when she still walked the hallway outside this very room. She had known she might not get another spring, and she had brought the tool anyway, like a promise.

"Visiting hours ended twenty minutes ago," the nurse said gently from the doorway. "You can come back tomorrow for her things."

"We can't come back tomorrow," Alexander said. "Tomorrow is the day it has to be done. There's no other day like it." His mother looked up, and something crossed her face, and then she said, "Get your coats."

The twist came at the cemetery gate, where the caretaker stopped them and said the family plot was locked until noon for maintenance. Alexander stood holding the broom, wondering whether the whole plan would collapse over a padlock, until Anayah noticed the caretaker staring at the worn handle.

"That's Old Chen's widow's broom," the caretaker said. "Your grandmother swept that stone every April fourth or fifth for fifty years. Never missed one." He unlocked the gate himself, without another word.

They swept the stone clean, and Alexander left an offering of sunflower seeds, her favorite. As they walked back down the hill, Antoine asked, "Do you think she knows we did it?"

Alexander looked back at the broom marks in the gravel, straight and even, like handwriting. "Ask me next April," he said.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: On a standard 400-metre outdoor track, the 800 metres is exactly two laps, so runners plan the race as a first lap and a second lap.
story:
Dominic stood at the gate of the community pool, looking past the water to the flat cinder path that looped around the whole complex. The path was measured, the coach had said, at four hundred metres around, exactly like a standard outdoor track, which meant the eight-hundred-metre race he'd signed up for next Saturday was two laps. Two. That number sat in his head all week like a stone, because last month he had blown the same race at school by sprinting the whole first lap and then dying in the second, legs heavy as wet towels.

Luc and Maxx were already stretched out on the hot concrete near the deep end, and Mr. Robinson, who ran the pool and had once raced in college, was raking the far side of the path. "Watch me," Luc said, standing up. "I'm going to beat your time today." He peeled off toward the gate, and Dominic counted his laps out loud as Luc pounded past. First lap. Luc looked strong, arms pumping, breathing hard but steady.

Then, coming around the second time, Luc kicked. He surged into a sprint, face clenched, and drove himself across the line by the concession stand before folding over his knees, gasping and grinning. "Won it," he panted. Dominic stared at him. "That was one lap. You've still got another whole lap to go." Luc's grin went sour, and something corrosive crept into his voice as he argued, but Dominic was barely listening. So that was how it happened. You lost count, you kicked for the finish a lap too early, and the race was gone.

The logic of it fell into place for Dominic right there on the pool deck. The eight hundred wasn't one long sprint; it was a first lap and a second lap, and they were different animals. First lap: fast but held back, saving something. Second lap: everything left, poured out all at once. He thought about the school race, the moment he had chosen to go flat out at the start, and he couldn't decide if that had been brave or just dumb. Maybe both. He wanted a do-over, and now he had one.

"Luc, count for me," he said, and walked to the gate. He started the first lap under control, lungs working but not burning, watching the shimmer of the pool slide past on his left. When he came around to the start again, he heard Luc call, "One left," and he let the brakes off, arms driving, gravel spitting from his heels as he went.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: A ball that rolls 3 meters in 2 seconds has an average speed of 1.5 meters per second.
story:
Hayden crouched at the top of the skate park's smallest ramp with a tennis ball in one hand and his dad's old stopwatch in the other. Bridget stood beside him holding the end of a tape measure, stretching it along the flat concrete until it reached the third mark. Three meters exactly.

"Ready?" Hayden called down to Vaughn, who knelt at the far end with his phone out to film it, because last time they had argued about whether the stopwatch was even close. "On three. One, two, three." He let the ball go and pressed the button at the same instant. The ball wobbled, curved a little toward the drain grate, and rolled past Vaughn's sneaker. Hayden stopped the watch. Two seconds. He wrote it in his notebook: 3 m, 2 s.

Here was the problem. Mr. Janssen had assigned a distance-time graph, and Hayden needed a speed in meters per second to draw the line. He stared at the two numbers, feeling the way he had in math class last month when a word problem about a train refused to open up for him. That time, the answer had come from cutting the problem into pieces he could actually picture. So he tried it now, out loud, mostly to himself. "Three meters, two seconds. If I split the meters between the seconds, each second gets one and a half." He checked it the other way around, stacking one and a half, then one and a half again, and landing on three. One point five meters per second. His pencil moved before he could second-guess himself.

"Say that again?" Bridget said, walking back up the ramp.

"It's going one point five meters per second," Hayden said. "That's the number for the graph."

"You sound like a math book," Vaughn said, but he was grinning, and the grin was contagious, because soon all three of them were laughing on the ramp in the late sun.

They ran the ball twice more so the graph would have more than one point. The second roll was slower, and the third went crooked and refused to cooperate, drifting off the tape measure entirely so that Vaughn had to chase it between two bikes. Hayden plotted the good rolls anyway: a steep little line, then a shallower one, both climbing from zero. He taped the graph paper to the ramp's metal edge so the wind wouldn't take it.

At home that evening he remembered being six, rolling a ball down the porch steps and trying to guess how fast it was going, and guessing wrong every single time. His dad had said, "You can't see speed, buddy. You have to catch it." Hayden hadn't understood then. He understood now.

The next morning he brought the notebook to Mr. Janssen's room and set it on the desk, open to the graph, with the stopwatch beside it.

"Three meters," Hayden said, "two seconds, one point five meters per second. I caught it."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun also gets longer days, giving sunlight more hours to warm the ground.
story:
Alexis dragged the soccer ball, the flashlight, and a garden stake out to the backyard, because tomorrow she had to explain the seasons to Mr. Takahashi's class, and right now she could not explain them to a houseplant. Her dad would commute an hour each way to the city and still make more sense at dinner than she made in her draft notes, which read, in full, "tilt, something something, summer."

Ishaan arrived first, holding two juice boxes like an offering. Alessio came next, still wearing his swim bag, because his little sister's lesson had been at the pool near the estuary and his mom had sent him straight over. "Okay," Alexis said. "Earth." She pointed at the soccer ball. "Sun." She held up the flashlight. "Ishaan, tilt the ball with the stake through it, like a skewer."

"Last year," Ishaan said, steadying the stake, "I told Mr. Takahashi summer happens because Earth gets closer to the Sun. He made that face. You know the face."

"The face is acute," Alessio said solemnly. "Like a ninety-degree angle of disappointment."

Alexis shone the flashlight straight on and turned off her brain's complaining and turned on the watching part. The light spread in a bright oval on one side of the ball. "Okay, so when the axis tilts, one hemisphere leans toward the Sun. That's us in summer, half of the..." She stopped. Something was off. The lit patch was bigger on the tilted-in side, sure, but the shine itself looked exactly as bright on the other half when she flipped it. If it wasn't brighter, then what was actually doing the work?

"Wait," she said slowly. "Flip it." Ishaan tipped the stake so the other half of the ball leaned in. Alexis traced the boundary between light and dark with her finger, around and around, and on the tilted-in half her finger traveled a longer path through light. "Look. The half leaning toward the Sun is lit for more of the spin. More of each day is daytime."

Alessio frowned. "So the ground gets more hours of sunlight to warm up."

"Longer days," Alexis said, "means the Sun has more hours to warm the ground. That's the actual thing. Not hotter sunshine. More sunshine per day." She sat back on the grass, feeling the evening air on her arms. "This summer at camp they made us go to bed before dark. I was so mad. Lights out at nine and the sky was still orange. That was this. The whole thing, and I was mad about it."

Ishaan grinned. "You were mad at the tilt of Earth's axis."

"I was mad at the axis," Alexis agreed. "In my defense, I didn't know it had a name."

She tried the explanation out loud once, start to finish, flashlight sweeping, ball tilting, and it hung together, every piece clicking into the next. Tomorrow she would stand up in front of everyone and say it, and if Mr. Takahashi made the face anyway, well, she had a flashlight, a soccer ball, and two witnesses. Alessio raised a juice box in salute. "To the axis," he said. "Enemy of bedtime, hero of summer."

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: The blues scale is the minor pentatonic scale with one extra note, the flattened fifth, which gives the music its gritty 'blue' sound.
story:
The music room smelled like old carpet and valve oil, and Connor had been stuck on the same twelve bars for a week. He could play the chord progression fine. He could even play the five notes his sheet called the minor pentatonic scale. But every solo he attempted sounded like a doorbell with ambitions, not the blues.

"You're playing it safe," said Phoebe, who was sprawled on the piano bench eating pretzels she wasn't supposed to have in here. "Real blues players sound like they're mad at the guitar."

"Marko doesn't sound mad at the guitar," Connor said. Marko had tried the solo yesterday and made it look easy, which was typical.

"Marko could sound mad at a sandwich," Phoebe said. "Some people just have it. You have to figure out where it hides."

Connor noodled the five notes again. They were fine. They were also boring, and he knew the boringness was coming from somewhere he couldn't see, like a smell in a fridge. There had to be a rule he was missing, something that turned notes into blues. He decided to test the only idea he had, which was to sneak one wrong note in on purpose, right in the middle, just to hear what would happen. If it sounded bad, fine, at least he'd know. He found the fifth note of the scale and dropped his finger down one fret.

The note came out gritty. Crooked. Kind of venomous, actually, like it had an attitude problem. He played the lick again and this time the whole solo seemed to lean. Phoebe sat up so fast she dropped a pretzel.

"What was that?" she said.

"That note," Connor said. "The flat one. It's not on my sheet."

Phoebe pulled out her phone, consulted it like a lawyer, and read: "Okay, this says the blues scale is the minor pentatonic with one extra note, the flattened fifth. That's literally the whole difference. You just found the blue part."

Connor tried to replicate his accident, slowly, then faster, threading the flat fifth through the twelve bars until the solo sounded like something you'd hear in a smoky club, if the club were a carpeted music room with a broken tambourine in the corner. That was when the door opened and Ms. Levy came in carrying a stack of folders, and Marko behind her, back early from his lesson.

"Marko wanted the last five minutes," Ms. Levy said, and began a brief negotiation about who got the room, which Phoebe handled by pointing at Connor and saying, "He's having a moment."

Marko leaned against the door, listening, arms crossed. When Connor finished, Marko didn't say anything for a second. Then he said, "How long have you known about that note?"

"About four minutes," Connor said.

Marko picked up the second guitar, plugged it in, and sat down across from him. "Play those bars again," he said. "But this time, you take the odd bars and I'll take the even ones."

"Then what?"

"Then we argue over whose turn it is," said Marko, and counted them in.

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: After the 1929 crash, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell about 89 percent from its September 1929 peak to its low in July 1932.
story:
Anna set the pitcher on the card table and weighted the price sign with a rock so the wind would stop flipping it over. The lemonade was real, squeezed that morning, unlike the synthetic lemon flavor Teo liked, which tasted like lemon but came from a factory. He was already at the end of the driveway with his math homework spread on his skateboard, which he was trying to earn money to replace.

"Five dollars for this stand," Anna said. "I'm keeping the profits."

"For what?" Teo asked.

"Grandpa Ed says I should invest it. He gave me a worksheet. One side says stock, one side says bond, and I have to write which is riskier and why." She poured him a cup he hadn't paid for yet.

Ms. Sutton came down the sidewalk with her watering can and stopped at the stand. "Lemonade and homework," she said. "That's a combination."

"Homework's the slow part," Anna said. "I know a stock is a piece of a company and a bond is a loan to it. I just can't see why anyone would call one riskier, since both can go down."

Ms. Sutton paid for a cup and drank half of it standing there, but she didn't answer the question. She was like that. She would water her flowers while you figured things out yourself.

Teo turned a worksheet page with his pencil. "Ask your mom about the family thing," he said. "The one you were telling me about. Your great-grandpa."

Anna had almost forgotten. Her mother had a box of old papers from Great-Grandpa Henry, including a bank envelope with a note in pencil. He had put his savings into stocks, and in the autumn of 1929 the market crashed. Anna had copied one line from a library book into her notebook and she got it out now, flattened on the table between the cups. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell about 89 percent from its September 1929 peak to its low in July 1932. She made Teo read it twice.

"Eighty-nine percent," Teo said. "So if he had a hundred dollars, he ended with eleven?"

"About that," Anna said. She scrutinized the number, then the bond column of her worksheet. If Henry had lent the company money instead, the company would still have owed him, even in a bad stretch. The paper said a bond was a promise to pay back. A stock wasn't a promise of anything. It was only worth what somebody would pay for it that day, and after 1929 almost nobody would pay much. She wrote at the bottom of the page: A stock is riskier because its price can fall almost all the way to nothing, like 89 percent, and nobody owes you the difference. She showed it to Teo.

Teo pushed his skateboard aside. "Okay, but here's my problem. I need sixty dollars and I've got fourteen. If I give you my fourteen and you owe me sixty by August, is that a bond?"

"That's a terrible bond," Anna said.

"It's a Teo bond. Sixty by August or I take the pitcher."

Ms. Sutton finished her cup and set it down. "I'll take one more," she said. "It's better than the powdered kind."

Anna poured it and put the two quarters in the coffee can, next to the pencil note that said Teo, $46, due August.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: To clear a fraction from an equation, multiply both sides by its denominator: if x divided by 3 equals 5, multiplying both sides by 3 gives x = 15.
story:
Brooke slapped the pizza receipt onto the kitchen table and pointed at the total, which was smudged beyond reading. "Okay, we each paid five dollars, three of us, so there has to be a way to figure out what the whole thing cost." Matis pulled out her phone calculator, but Zayne slid his math notebook across the table before she could tap a single button.

"Wait, wait. This is exactly what Ms. Fernando has been drilling us on all week." He wrote x over 3 equals 5 in big letters, then circled it. "It's cumulative, too, everything since September leads to this one trick." Brooke leaned over his shoulder, chewing the end of her pencil. The x was the total, hidden under that smudge, and the 3 underneath it meant the cost had been split three ways. Each share was five dollars.

"So the smudge is x," Brooke said slowly, and then her pencil started moving before she'd fully decided what to do. She wrote the equation again in her own handwriting, then multiplied the left side by 3 and, because something in her head insisted fairness mattered even in arithmetic, multiplied the right side by 3 as well. The threes on the left cancelled each other out, and x sat alone next to 15. She sat back so fast her chair scraped the floor. "Fifteen. The whole pizza was fifteen dollars!"

"Check it," Matis said, still holding her calculator like she didn't trust any of them. She divided 15 by 3 and got 5, which matched everyone's share exactly. Zayne whooped and did a drumroll on the table edge. "You just cleared the fraction. Multiply both sides by the denominator and the fraction disappears. That's the whole move."

Brooke was already flipping to a fresh page, hungry for more. "Let's do a harder one. What if it's split four ways and each share is seven?" She wrote it out fast, x over 4 equals 7, and Matis grabbed a second pencil to race her. Zayne kept time on his phone like a referee.

"You know," Matis said between problems, "I always had this stereotype in my head that algebra was for lonely geniuses with chalkboards. This is way better. This is pizza math." When Brooke beat her to the answer on the third problem, Matis groaned and dropped her pencil, and Brooke reached over to console her by sliding the last slice of leftover pizza onto her plate.

"Winner shares," Brooke said, and spun her pencil once through her fingers. "Now give me another one."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: A primary source is something made at the time by a person who lived through an event, such as a settler's diary, while a secondary source is written later by someone studying it.
story:
The worksheet was due at the end of the field trip, and Zoe had forty minutes left to find a primary source about why settlers moved west in the 1800s. She stood in the museum's trail exhibit with her pencil hovering over the blank box marked "Source."

"Grab the textbook in the gift shop," Teo said, pointing at a shiny paperback titled Westward Expansion: A History. "It says everything. Land, gold, the whole list."

Zoe picked it up anyway and flipped to the middle. The chapters had dates like 1998 under the author's name, and sentences like "Historians believe the railroad was the main factor." She set it back on the shelf. Something about it felt secondhand, like being told about a movie instead of watching it.

"It's written later," she said slowly. "By someone studying it. That makes it a secondary source. I need something made at the time, by a person who actually lived through it." She wasn't entirely sure that distinction mattered, but her intuition said the assignment did.

In the glass case near the oxen cart sat a small leather diary, open to a page from 1852. The museum label said it belonged to a farm wife who walked from Ohio. Zoe leaned close to read the faded ink. "The bank took the farm in spring. Samuel says the soil in Oregon is free to anyone who will work it. I am afraid of the river crossings, but staying here is worse." Her pencil started moving, generating three quick sentences before she could second-guess them. She wrote down why the family left, straight from the woman's own hand.

Jade appeared at her elbow, frowning at her half-filled worksheet. "I used that movie in the theater room. Is that primary?"

"Was the narrator there in the 1800s?" Zoe asked.

"No. He's a narrator."

Jade sighed and went back toward the exhibit cases, and Zoe followed her, because there was one question left on the sheet and she wanted to help. Together they found a stack of letters in another case, written by a soldier at a fort in 1860. "These work," Zoe said. "Letters count too. Made at the time, by the person living it."

The bus horn sounded in the parking lot. Jade scribbled her answer, and Zoe checked her own page one last time, where the diary's careful handwriting was copied into the box. At the door, Mr. Mansour collected the worksheets and paused over Zoe's page.

"Nice choice," he said. "That diary is exactly the kind of thing historians get excited about."

Zoe looked back once at the little leather book in its case, thinking of the woman who had written it, vulnerable and hopeful on a muddy trail, and waved at the glass as she walked out.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Wool shrinks in hot, sloshing water because tiny scales on each wool fibre open up and lock onto neighbouring fibres, pulling the knit tighter. This is called felting.
story:
Grayson stood in his grandma's laundry room holding a basket that smelled like lavender and old rain. His grandma had broken her wrist, so for the whole week he was in charge of washing everything, and he meant to do it properly. He sorted the clothes into piles on the floor: dark jeans here, white towels there, a heap of colors in between. His friend Phoenix had come along for the afternoon and sat on the dryer, swinging his legs.

"Hot water for the whites," Grayson said, reading the dial. "Cold for the dark stuff. That's the rule."

Phoenix pointed at a woolly green sweater folded on the shelf. "What about that one?"

"That's Grandpa's. He knitted it himself last winter." Grayson lifted it. It was heavy and soft, with a collar the size of a dinner plate. His instinct said wool probably wasn't like towels, but the pile of colors was right there, and the machine was already set to hot. He shrugged and dropped the sweater in with everything else. The drum filled, sloshed, and churned while the two boys went to the kitchen for sandwiches.

When the load finished, Grayson pulled the clothes out one by one. The jeans were fine. The towels were fine. Then his hand touched the sweater, and his stomach dropped. It had shrunk to the size of a doll's coat. The collar that had been a dinner plate now wouldn't fit around his forearm.

"Oh no," Phoenix said. "Oh no, oh no."

Grayson laid it flat on the counter and stared. He hadn't cut it, hadn't burned it, hadn't done anything but wash it. So something invisible had happened. Wool must have a hidden rule. He found his grandma's magnifying glass in the junk drawer and tugged a single loose fibre from the sweater's cuff, pinching it straight. Under the glass he could just see that the fibre wasn't smooth. It was covered in tiny scales, like a fish or a pinecone.

"Look," he said. Phoenix leaned in. "They're like little hooks. If they open up, maybe they grab the fibres next to them and pull everything tighter."

"So it's not that the wool got smaller," Phoenix said slowly. "It's that it got pulled together."

Grayson grabbed his notebook. He needed one more test before he told his grandma anything. He had a small square of knitted wool, leftover from the same yarn in her basket, and he cut it in half. One half he soaked in cold water in a bowl. The other he swished in a pot of hot water, sloshing it around with a spoon the way the machine would have. After ten minutes he laid both squares side by side. The cold one was the same size. The hot, sloshed one had shrunk almost a quarter, and it felt stiffer and denser, like felt.

"That's it," Grayson said. "Hot, sloshing water makes the scales open and lock on. Cold water, they stay closed."

His grandma came in with her cast propped on a pillow and heard the whole story, then held up the tiny sweater and laughed until she had to sit down. "That's called felting, love," she said. "Grandpa's going to wear it as a joke on his birthday." She looked at the shrunken square in his notebook and added, "You tested it properly, though. That's more than most scientists do."

The next morning, Grayson washed a second load, all by the rules he had written down. He kept the water cold for anything wool, hung the sweaters to dry flat, folded the towels into neat squares, and carried the basket out to the tranquil back porch where his grandpa sat in the sun. Grandpa tried on the tiny sweater, and it fit exactly one of his hands, like a green mitten with a collar. He wiggged his fingers inside it and grinned.

"Next one," Grandpa said, "wash it in cold. And Grayson, could you teach me to fold like that? Mine always come out as lumps."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Fire-safety guidance says to put out a campfire by drowning it with water, stirring the ashes, and drowning it again until everything is cool to the touch.
story:
The minivan was packed, and Daniel had his seatbelt on when he smelled it. Smoke. He turned around and looked through the back window at the fire pit, where a thin gray thread was still rising from the ashes. "Dad, the fire's not out," he said. His father put the keys on the dashboard and got out, and Daniel climbed over Isa's duffel bag and followed him.

Isa, who had come along on the trip, trailed after them with the last water bottle. "It's just ashes," she said. "Ashes can't burn." Daniel crouched at the edge of the pit anyway and held his palm above it, not touching. Heat came off it in waves, steady as a radiator. "Something down there is still hot," he said. He remembered the folded paper the ranger had handed them at check-in, still crumpled in his pocket from three days ago. He flattened it against his knee. The paper said to drown the fire with water, stir the ashes, and drown it again until everything was cool to the touch. He read the line twice, because it was oddly specific. Drown, stir, drown. He'd assumed you just poured water once and walked away, and now he could see why that might not work. Water poured on top would slide off. Stirring would break the ashes open and let the water get underneath.

He tipped the water bottle over the pit. Steam hissed up in a white cloud, and the smell of wet ash filled the air. He found a stick as long as his arm and dragged it through the pile, flipping chunks over. Underneath, one lump glowed dull orange, like a coal in a fireplace. Isa pointed at it. "There. That's the problem." Daniel poured again until the glow went gray. Then he stirred a second time, turning everything over, hunting for more orange. There was none. He counted to thirty in his head and touched the back of his hand to the largest chunk. Still warm, like a mug of cocoa left sitting. Not safe. He got the second water bottle from the cooler in the trunk and drowned it a third time.

While they worked, Isa sat on the picnic table bench playing the card game they'd invented on rainy Tuesday, the one where you win points by dismantling your opponent's setup one card at a time. "You look like a peasant digging a well," she said, watching him hunch over the pit with the stick. "A peasant who takes his well very seriously." Daniel didn't answer. He stirred, poured, and touched again. This time the ash was cool, cool all the way through, even where the orange lump had been. He checked every chunk he could find, because the paper had said everything, not most things, and "most of the fire is out" seemed like the kind of sentence nobody wanted to say right before a forest burned down.

They stood there a minute longer and watched the pit, but nothing moved and nothing smoked. It looked like nothing at all, gray and flat and dead. "Dad, it passed the touch test," Daniel called over. "Cool to the touch." His father came and pressed his own hand to the ash, then nodded once, which from him was significant praise.

Back in the minivan, Daniel buckled in next to Isa and his father turned the key. "Fifteen seconds ago we would have driven off and left that pit hot," his father said, backing out of the campsite. "Stir, drown, stir," Isa said, dealing the cards onto the console between the seats. "Your move, peasant."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, lines that face you squarely, like window tops and doorframes on a building's front, stay perfectly horizontal or vertical.
story:
Megan pressed her pencil so hard against the paper that the tip snapped. The art room smelled like chalk dust and old tempera paint, and outside the windows a February wind rattled the glass, nothing like the tropical beach on the poster Mr. Reyes had pinned above the sink. She had twenty minutes left before the bell, and her street drawing looked wrong in a way she couldn't name.

"Mine's done," said Myah, holding up her page. Myah wanted the ribbon at the district show more than anything, and she had drawn a neat row of shops that all slanted wildly to the left. "See how I made every line angle toward the dot? Mr. Reyes said lines go to the vanishing point."

"That's the sidewalk edges," Megan said slowly. "And the rooflines on the sides." She looked from Myah's paper to the actual view out the window, where the brick building across the street faced them square on. Its window tops ran flat and level, like a ruler laid across the wall. Its doorframe stood straight up and down, even though she could see the whole front of it plainly. She grabbed Myah's page and held it beside the window. "Look at the real building. The front of it doesn't lean anywhere."

Myah frowned. "Then why do my shops look like they're falling over?"

"Because you slanted the tops of the windows and the doorframes," Megan said. She was guessing, but it felt like a guess worth testing. She pulled her own paper close and erased her crooked shopfront, then redrew the windows with a ruler, tops perfectly horizontal, sides perfectly vertical, while the diagonal lines of the sidewalk and rooftops raced off toward her vanishing point. When she held the page at arm's length, the street suddenly had depth. The shops stood firm and the road pulled her eye straight toward the dot.

"Ten minutes," Mr. Reyes called from his desk, where he was sorting brushes into a bin for the ones too worn to retire.

"Fix yours," Megan said, sliding the ruler across the table to Myah. "Horizontal tops, straight-up doorframes. Try one window and see."

Myah redrew a single window top level, then the doorframe beneath it, and her whole street steadied. "It's like a little revolution on the page," she whispered.

"Five minutes," said Mr. Reyes.

Megan shaded the last window, her pencil whispering across the paper, and the street ran on and on toward its far-off point.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: In both 1995 and 1996 David Justice had a higher batting average than Derek Jeter, yet Jeter's average for the two years combined was higher.
story:
The bleachers shook under Emily every time the home crowd stomped, but she barely noticed. She had her dad's phone balanced on her knee, showing Quincy the batting averages she'd found for a school project on sports stats. "Look, 1995. David Justice, .253. Derek Jeter, .250. Justice wins." She scrolled down. "And 1996. Justice again, .321 to .314. Justice wins both years."

"Then Justice is obviously better," Quincy said. He wanted to pick a winner so he could print the name on his poster in giant letters before the fourth quarter ended, because Ms. Ross had promised the best project would hang in the hallway. He reached for the phone. "Just give me the guy who won."

"Wait." Emily's thumb had stopped on the combined numbers at the bottom of the page. "That can't be right." She read the line twice, then a third time. "For the two years together, Jeter is higher. Jeter, .300 to .270."

Quincy snatched the phone and squinted at it. "That's a typo. How can Justice win every year and lose when you put the years together?" On the court below, someone missed a free throw and the crowd groaned, but Emily was somewhere else entirely, turning the problem over like a stone with something hidden underneath. One number for one year, one number for another year, and then a different number when you stacked them. Same player, same bat. How did the answer change depending on how you counted?

She grabbed a napkin from the snack bag and started writing the years in columns. "Every average is a whole season squeezed into one number," she said slowly, mostly to herself. "A ranking is the same thing, right? First place or second place, one number, and a hundred games behind it." She tapped the napkin. "The news does this too. Player rankings, percentages, everything squished down." Quincy watched her scribble, his resentment plain on his face, because she was taking his quick answer and stretching it into a mystery. "If we put Jeter on the poster," he said, "somebody's going to say we're wrong. The numbers for each year say Justice."

"Then we show all the numbers," Emily said. "The yearly ones and the combined one, side by side, and let people see that they don't match up. That's more honest than picking a winner." She looked at him. "Ms. Ross said she wanted something objective, right? Just the facts?"

Quincy thought about it while a three-point shot arced through the net and the gym exploded with stomping. Then he grinned and pulled a marker from his backpack. "Fine. But the poster headline is mine to write." He printed in huge letters across the top of a clean sheet: WHO REALLY WON? Emily leaned over and added underneath, in smaller letters, 1995: Justice. 1996: Justice. Two years combined: Jeter.

"Read it out loud," she said.

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: The pH scale was introduced in 1909 by Danish chemist Søren Sørensen, who worked at the Carlsberg Laboratory in Copenhagen.
story:
Emilia pressed her nose against the glass case in the chemistry hall, where a strip of purple paper lay next to a bottle marked CARLSBERG LABORATORY. Behind her, Emmanuel was reading a placard out loud, but he kept stopping halfway through, so Irene leaned over his shoulder to finish it for him.

"I already told you," Irene said. "My cousin says pH was invented by a French guy. He learned it in high school."

"My dad says it was somebody at a beer company," Emmanuel said. "Which sounds made up, honestly."

Emilia wanted to know who was right, but she wanted something else more. She had three mystery liquids in front of her at the hands-on table: lemon juice, soapy water, and a cup the museum staff had labeled only with a question mark. Her task card said to use litmus paper to sort each one as an acid or a base. The purple strips sat in a shallow dish, and a rainbow-colored chart on the wall showed numbers from zero to fourteen.

She dipped a strip into the lemon juice. It turned pink, fast, like tropical sunset colors creeping across the paper. She held it up next to the chart. "Zero to one," she said. "Definitely an acid." The soapy water turned the strip blue and greenish, way up near the high numbers, which meant a base. Irene tried the mystery cup, and the strip barely changed at all, hovering right around the middle, neither one thing nor the other.

"So it's broken," Irene said.

"It's not broken. It's just neutral," Emilia said. "Like water." She speculated for a moment that the museum had filled the cup with plain water on purpose, to see whether kids would guess or actually test. She wrote NEUTRAL on her worksheet with a stubby pencil that smelled like the lemon juice had splashed it.

Then the argument started up again, louder this time, and a man at the next table glanced over. Emilia walked back to the glass case and read the placard all the way through, slowly, the way Ms. Lau had taught her to read primary sources instead of trusting what people remembered.

"The pH scale was introduced in 1909 by Søren Sørensen," she read, "a Danish chemist who worked at the Carlsberg Laboratory in Copenhagen."

"See? A beer company," Emmanuel said.

"Carlsberg," Emilia said. "In Copenhagen. So your dad was right, and Irene's cousin was wrong." She copied the name into her notebook, letter by letter, because Sørensen had two letters she always got mixed up. Irene looked at the placard herself, sighed, and said her cousin was going to hear about this.

On their way out, Emilia stopped at the question-mark cup one more time and dipped a fresh strip in, just to watch it stay the same stubborn purple, balanced in the middle.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Around June 21, the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer; around December 21, it is directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn.
story:
Zack crouched at the edge of the old rock quarry, pressing a stick upright into a patch of gravel between two slabs covered in orange lichen. His science project was due Monday morning, and it had to answer one question: what causes the seasons? He had written "we're closer to the Sun in summer" on his draft, and Mr. Adeyemi had circled it in red and written "test this" beside it. So here he was on a Saturday, with a stick, a tape measure, and two hours before his ride home.

Marwan climbed down after him, holding a globe borrowed from the classroom. Gabryel came last, checking her watch every few minutes because soccer tryouts started at four. "I budgeted exactly forty minutes for this," she said. "If it takes longer, I'm running up the trail."

Marwan set the globe on a flat stone and spun it slowly. "There are two dotted lines on this thing," he said, tracing one with his finger. "Tropic of Cancer, and way down here, Tropic of Capricorn. What do they even mark?"

Zack stared at the lines. He remembered his cousin saying something about them once, something about the Sun. He pulled out his notebook and found the page from the library book he'd copied. Around June 21, the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. Around December 21, it's directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn.

"Directly overhead," Zack said. "That means no shadow at noon, right there, on those lines." He pointed at his own stick. "We're not on either line. So if the seasons were about distance, shadows would be the same all year and the Sun would sit overhead everywhere. But it doesn't. It only sits straight overhead on those lines, and only on those dates. That means the Sun's position in the sky moves." He tapped the tilted globe. "Because the axis is tilted." The Earth leaned, and the lean decided where the noon Sun stood.

"Prove it," Gabryel said, arms crossed.

"Watch the shadow from morning to noon," Zack said. "It shrinks until noon, then grows again. Now imagine marking its noon length every month. Shortest near June 21, longest near December 21. Same tilt, same lean, swinging the overhead spot between those two lines." He planted a second stick at an angle to show the tilt, and Marwan crouched to sight along it. "The book never said why," Zack admitted. "Just that it happens there, on those dates."

Gabryel checked her watch again and stood. "Thirty-five minutes gone. That's good enough for me." Then she stopped, halfway up the trail, and turned around. "Wait. Your whole project is wrong for one more reason. If we're closer to the Sun in our summer, then December would be summer in Australia. Is it?"

Marwan was already flipping the globe to the bottom half. "It is. When the Sun's over the Tropic of Capricorn, it's their summer."

Zack wrote one word at the top of his notebook, crossed out his first draft entirely, and started measuring the shadow.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: When viewing a slide, you start with the lowest-power objective lens to find and focus on the cells before switching to higher power.
story:
Arthur twisted the smallest knob on the microscope and squinted into the eyepiece again. Gray blur, nothing else, like looking through a shower door. The clock above the museum lab read 1:40, and the bus back to school left at 2:00 sharp, which gave him twenty minutes to draw an onion cell and label the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus before Ms. Cruz collected the worksheets at the door.

"You have to start with the little lens," said Loralie at the next station, not even looking up from her own slide. "The small one. Find the cells first, then switch up."

Arthur remembered the microscope unit back in fifth grade, when he had cranked the big objective down in one confident twist and cracked a slide belonging to Francis. Francis had been cool about it, but the teacher hadn't, and Arthur had spent the rest of the period washing beakers. He'd told himself then that he would never touch a microscope carelessly again, though here he was, doing exactly the opposite. Some promises, he thought, don't correspond to what you actually do when the clock is running.

He clicked the lowest-power lens into place, the short one. The blur shrank. He turned the coarse knob slowly, and shapes swam up out of the gray, rows of boxes like bricks in a wall. Onion cells. He felt his shoulders drop an inch. Now he switched to the higher power, and the boxes grew, each one showing a darker dot near its edge. The nucleus. The outer line, thick and firm, had to be the cell wall; just inside it, a thinner boundary hugged the edge, and he drew that as the membrane, labeling them with his smallest letters.

"Ten minutes," Ms. Cruz called.

Across the table, Francis was hunched over his paper, frowning at his eyepiece. "Mine's all purple blobs," he muttered. Arthur leaned over. Francis had the high-power lens locked in, hunting through blur for cells that were nowhere in view. Arthur almost laughed, then remembered the beakers. He pointed at the lens turret. "Smallest lens first. Then the big one." Francis clicked it over, focused, and let out a breath like he'd been underwater.

But when Arthur slid his own slide out to compare, he stopped. Francis's cells were long and pointed, like arrows, not brick boxes at all. Loralie came over and read the label on Francis's slide. "That says elodea. It's a leaf, not onion." Francis stared at his drawing, then back at the slide tray, where a second slide, mislabeled, sat beside the true onion one. Somebody at the museum had switched the labels, and for one second Arthur wondered which of his own neatly labeled parts might not correspond to anything real at all.

"Bus," said Ms. Cruz from the doorway.

Arthur handed in his paper and, at the last second, added one small word next to the nucleus: "probably."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Historians sort reasons for migration into push factors, which drive people away from home, and pull factors, which attract them to a new place.
story:
Quinn slid the slim green book across the library table and kept her hand on top of it, as if Hayden might snatch it away. "Mr. Côté appointed me keeper of the diary, so nobody licks their fingers before turning pages." Hayden rolled his eyes, but he wiped his hands on his jeans anyway. Zorawar pulled his chair closer, notebook open to a fresh page.

The assignment was due Friday: use one primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. Mr. Côté had dug the diary out of the local history shelf, the 1847 record of the Merritt family, who had left Missouri for Oregon. Their teacher had called it a gold mine, and now Quinn understood why, because the middle of the book held a folded letter, tucked between the pages like a bookmark.

Quinn read it aloud in a low voice, since the library was quiet and a parent volunteer was shelving books nearby. "My dear Ruth, I am writing to beg you not to go. Your father says the land is worn out, but land can be healed if a body is patient. The baby is too small for such a road. Stay until spring at least. Your loving mother." Nobody said anything for a moment. Zorawar tapped his pencil twice, then started writing fast.

"So what do we have so far?" Quinn said. "The teacher wants reasons, sorted." Zorawar held up his notebook. "I made two columns. Worn-out land, that pushes them away from Missouri. And there's the pamphlet Mr. Côté copied, the one with the extravagant promises about Oregon, free land and rich soil everywhere. That pulls them." Hayden frowned. "Push and pull," Quinn said slowly, trying the words out. "Some reasons push you out of home, and some pull you toward the new place." She wrote PUSH at the top of one column and PULL at the top of the other, then added the grandmother's worry to neither column, because worry was not a reason, it was a weight.

They worked through the diary page by page. Fever in the county pushed them out. A brother already in Oregon pulled them west. Drought pushed; a letter from the brother claiming the wheat grew taller than a man pulled, though Hayden pointed out that brothers brag. Then Quinn stopped at the last entry before the family left, and read it twice, because it changed everything.

"Listen. 'Ruth's cough is worse in the wet season, and Doctor Ames says the dry air beyond the mountains may ease her lungs. We will not tell her mother this, for she would say we chase a cure like fools.'" Quinn looked up. "She was sick. Ruth, the one who wrote the diary. That's why they're really going." Hayden sat back. "So all the free land stuff, the pull, is half a cover story. The big reason is a push, just one nobody can see in a tax record or whatever." Zorawar drew an arrow from one column to the other and wrote beside it: hidden push.

Quinn tested the idea against the diary like checking a math answer. If the family was pulled mainly by free land, they would have waited for spring, when travel was easier. They left in late summer instead, which made sense only if a sick person needed dry air before another wet Missouri winter arrived. Cause and effect lined up, and a chill went up her arms that had nothing to do with the library's cold air vent. People had been doing their homework on the Merritts for a century, apparently, and none of them had found this page, or none of them had cared about a girl named Ruth.

When the bell rang, Quinn carried the diary to the front desk herself. Mr. Côté raised his eyebrows at the three of them still hovering. "You know," Quinn said, "the pull factors get all the attention. The pamphlets, the promises. But sometimes the push is the whole story, and it's hiding in the last place anybody checks." Mr. Côté took the book, and for a second he held it the way you hold something fragile. "Then put it in your report," he said. "Ruth waited a hundred and seventy years for someone to notice her."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: The Sieve of Eratosthenes, an ancient Greek method, lists primes by crossing out the multiples of each prime in turn.
story:
The computer lab at Camp Winnowick smelled like sunscreen and warm keyboards, which Alexa thought was a weird combination for a place with no windows. She had signed up for coding because her brother said it was easy, and she now suspected he had lied, because her program kept telling her that 9 was prime.

"It is not prime," she muttered at the screen. "Nine is three times three. I know this."

Brantley leaned over from the next computer, chewing a pretzel. "Then your code is sinister. It's plotting against you."

"My code is broken, not evil." She highlighted the loop again, hunting for the mistake. On her paper beside the keyboard was the assignment: write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime. Mr. Rowe, the camp's coding instructor, had promised a popsicle to anyone who finished before lunch, and Alexa cherished that popsicle already, lime if she could get it.

Kareem slid his chair over, holding a marker and a piece of graph paper covered in tiny numbers. "Stop staring at your screen for one second. Look." He had written the numbers 2 through 50 in a grid, and some were crossed out. "It's called the Sieve of Eratosthenes. This ancient Greek guy listed primes by crossing out the multiples of each prime in turn. Two, so cross out 4, 6, 8, all of them. Then 3, so 9, 15, everything already gone from 2 stays crossed. Then 5."

"Why are you doing math by hand when we have computers?" Brantley asked.

"Because," Kareem said, "if her program says 9 is prime and my sieve says it isn't, then we know exactly who's wrong." He tapped the 9 on his grid, crossed out when he did the threes.

Alexa felt the suspense tighten in her chest, the good kind, like waiting for a carnival ride to drop. She read her loop out loud, slowly, following it with her finger. "For each number from 2 up to n, if n divides evenly, it's not prime." Then she saw it. Her loop stopped too early, and her check had a typo, an equals sign where she needed two. "Oh no. I told it the wrong thing. I told it 9 divides evenly means prime. Backwards."

She fixed the line, saved, and typed 9. Not prime, the screen said. She typed 7. Prime. She typed 49, and Kareem hunted through his grid with the marker cap, found 49, and crossed it out. "Not prime," the program said, and Kareem's sieve agreed.

"Not prime," Kareem announced, in the exact same robot voice as the computer.

Brantley raised his pretzel like a trophy. "The machine and the Greek agree. Popsicle time."

Alexa typed one more number, 2, the smallest prime of all, and hit enter with a flourish.

activity: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
knowledge_domain: to change a flat bicycle tyre using tyre levers and a pump
fact: A pinch flat, often called a snakebite, is two small parallel slits made when an under-inflated tyre hits a sharp edge like a kerb.
story:
Zoey wheeled her bike behind the grocery store and knelt beside the back wheel, which had gone soft as a loaf of squashed bread. She had ridden here on purpose, because the air pump stood next to the vending machines and because Ms. Menon, who worked the register, kept a box of patch kits behind the counter for neighbourhood kids.

"Let me guess," said Reese, who had followed her from the bike racks, grocery bag swinging. "Kerb?" Zoey nodded and popped the tyre off with the plastic levers, careful the way she had practised at home on an old wheel. She pulled out the inner tube and spun it slowly under the light.

The morning flashed back to her: she had been racing Ariella down Hillcrest, pumping hard, and when she hit the kerb at the corner the wheel had barked against the concrete edge. The tyre had felt a little squishy even before that, but she was winning, so she had accelerated instead of stopping.

Now, in the tube, she found them. Two small slits, neat and parallel, like a snake had sunk its fangs in twice. She held the tube up so Reese could see. "Look. Two holes, side by side. Why two?" She turned it over, thinking. A nail would make one hole. A thorn would make one. Two clean cuts that matched meant something had squeezed the tube from both sides at once. "I didn't run over glass," she said slowly. "I hit the kerb. And the tyre was low before that." She traced the holes with her finger. "So a soft tyre, hitting a hard edge... the tube gets pinched. That's why the cuts are parallel."

Reese leaned in. "My brother calls that a snakebite." Zoey grinned. Even the name made sense, fang marks side by side.

She roughed up the area with the sandpaper, pressed on a patch, and waited while Reese counted to sixty out loud, twice. Then she seated the tyre back on the rim with her thumbs, and only the levers when it fought her. At the pump she filled it until the tyre felt firm when she pressed with her thumb, then checked it again, harder. Not a temporary fix this time. She wanted it to hold all the way home and tomorrow too.

"That patch has a warranty?" Reese asked. "Nope," Zoey said. "The warranty is me checking the air every single morning." She swung her leg over the frame, and the tyre held a perfect round shadow on the pavement as she rolled out past the carts.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: A 2001 study that observed children on school playgrounds found that other children were present during 88 percent of bullying episodes.
story:
Jayden found the sentence on page 47 of a library book about playgrounds, of all things, while eating cereal at the kitchen table. In 2001, a study that observed children on school playgrounds found that other children were present during 88 percent of bullying episodes. He read it twice, then a third time, because his first thought was "so what" and his second thought was not that at all.

"Wesley," he said out loud to nobody, because Wesley was the whole problem. Every day at lunch a couple of kids imitated the way Wesley talked with his hands, and every day about nine other kids watched and did nothing, and every day Jayden was one of the nine. He had been counting himself as furniture. But if other children were there during 88 percent of episodes, then watchers weren't furniture. They were the scenery, and scenery was most of the show. If the scenery moved, the show changed.

He tested the idea on his mom that evening while she washed dishes. "Can I practice something on you?" She said sure, so he stood at the counter and pretended to be a kid at the next table, the one who usually laughed. She stood at the sink pretending to be a kid mocking Wesley's hands. "Cut it out, Wesley's fine," Jayden said, flat, like reporting the weather. His mom raised an eyebrow. "That's it?" "That's it. Not a speech. If I make a big flourish out of it, they'll tease him worse for having a bodyguard." She said that sounded plausible, turned off the tap, and told him he had a weird hobby.

Thursday he came home from school and flopped onto the couch where his dad was reading a memoir by some basketball player. "It worked," Jayden said. "Louis did it too. Somebody said something about Wesley's hands and I just said, 'That's old, find something else,' and Louis said, 'Yeah, honestly,' and the kid stopped." He had watched it happen like a science experiment. One sentence, then a second voice, and the whole table shifted, like turning a light on in a room everyone had been pretending was dark.

"Nine other kids saw it," Jayden added, staring at the ceiling. "Nine. And it only took two of us." His dad set down the memoir. "You want to tell me again slower, because that actually sounded like a plan." Jayden grinned and pulled the library book off the coffee table, opening it flat to page 47.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Many of the world's hot deserts lie near 30 degrees north or south of the equator, where sinking air warms up and dries out.
story:
Matteo sat cross-legged on his grandfather's braided rug, spinning the old globe with one finger while rain ticked against the window. On the kitchen table behind him lay his homework: two graphs, one showing monthly rainfall in the Sonoran Desert, the other in the Amazon rainforest, plus temperature lines that spiked and flattened like uneven skylines. He had promised Ms. Lau he would finish the comparison tonight, and tomorrow morning Lorelei would present their poster with whatever he handed her. He traced his finger over the globe and stopped. The Sahara. He turned it a bit. The Arabian Desert. A little more. The Kalahari, the Australian outback, the Atacama. They weren't scattered anywhere. They lined up in two bands, one above the equator and one below, like a belt worn twice.

"Nonno," he called, "do you have a marker that won't kill the globe?"

His grandfather shuffled in with a coffee cup and handed him a grease pencil. Matteo marked each desert. Then he fetched the atlas from the shelf, found the latitude scale printed along the margin, and measured. Sahara, about thirty degrees north. Arabian, about thirty. Kalahari, about twenty-some south, close to the same belt when he checked the map's finer lines. The deserts clustered near thirty degrees north or south of the equator, two coherent stripes running around the whole planet.

"So that's why the graph for the desert stays flat all year," Matteo said, mostly to himself. "It's not random dryness. It's a rule with an address."

He remembered, suddenly, the science quiz he had bombed in October. He'd guessed that deserts were dry because they were far from the ocean, and Ms. Lau had marked it wrong without comment. He'd been embarrassed, and he hadn't asked why. He glanced at the window. Maybe he should have asked. He still wasn't sure he would have, even now, if the globe hadn't done the asking for him.

He tested the idea against his rainforest graph. The Amazon sat almost on the equator, nowhere near thirty degrees, and its rainfall bars rose tall every single month. He turned back to the globe and spun it to thirty degrees south, over the Australian outback, then to thirty degrees north, over the Sahara again. Deserts there, rainforests not there. The pattern held every time he checked it. He tried to quantify it by counting: on his globe, nine deserts in the two belts, and only one, a small cold one, sitting anywhere else. His grandfather leaned over his shoulder.

"Nine out of ten," Matteo said. "The air must sink there or something. Sink, and dry out." He wrote it in the margin of his poster draft: many hot deserts lie near thirty degrees north or south of the equator, where sinking air warms up and dries out.

"That's more than I ever knew about deserts," his grandfather said, tapping the grease pencil against the Sahara.

Matteo photographed the marked globe for Lorelei, packed the graphs into his backpack, and left the globe on the table, deserts circling it in two thin grey rings.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: Every formula in Excel or Google Sheets begins with an equals sign; without it, the cell just shows what was typed as text.
story:
Mason slid into the chair beside Karter at the library computers and pulled up his spreadsheet with a grin he could not hold back. He had spent three evenings collecting data for the school fundraiser: bottles collected per homeroom, counted and typed into column B, rows stretching down to row ten.

"Watch this," he said. He clicked the empty cell at the bottom of the column and typed SUM(B2:B10). He pressed Enter.

The cell just sat there, showing SUM(B2:B10) in plain text, like a note to himself. Mason stared at it. Karter leaned in and frowned.

"That's not a number," Karter said.

"I know it's not a number." Mason clicked the cell again, then a random cell on Karter's sheet, where a total appeared as 412. Same idea, different result. So something about the two cells was different. He deleted the text and retyped it, letter by letter, watching each character appear. Still text. He looked closer at Karter's cell. In the formula bar at the top, before the word SUM, sat one small symbol Mason had skipped: an equals sign. He had assumed the program would recognize the word on its own, but maybe it needed to be told, right up front, that a formula was coming. Without that sign, the cell treated everything as ordinary words.

He typed =SUM(B2:B10) and hit Enter.

"Six hundred and thirty-eight bottles," he said, both hands in the air. "Karter. Six hundred and thirty-eight."

"Make the chart before you break something," Karter said, laughing. Mason highlighted the homeroom names and the numbers, clicked Insert, and chose a bar chart. Bars sprang up across the screen, one tall column towering over the rest.

"Ms. Szabó's homeroom is destroying everyone," Mason said. "Look at that. Almost double Karter's class."

Behind them, Ms. Szabó herself set down a returned book and peered at the screen. "Is that the bottle drive?"

"Yes, and the winner is obvious," Mason said. "Unless the coach wants to change the criterion to bottles per student, since homerooms aren't the same size."

"That would be arbitrary," Ms. Szabó said. "The rules were posted in September."

"Then I could add a second chart," Mason said, fingers already moving. "One for total, one for average. I can't build both myself by Friday, though."

"I'll take the averages," Karter said. "Delegate. That's what the tall bar means, right? You're the boss of the spreadsheet."

"You're the boss of one column," Mason said, and dragged the chart to the top of the sheet where everyone could see it.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Sprinting the first lap faster than a pace you can hold uses up quick anaerobic energy early, so the runner usually slows sharply on the second lap.
story:
Oliver had one week to figure out the eight hundred metres before Friday's time trial, and his problem was simple: every time he raced it, he died on the second lap. He led the first lap like a champion, and then his legs turned to wet sand and people streamed past him on the final straight. Sahil had watched it happen twice and said nothing, which somehow felt worse than teasing.

On Monday he stood at the track with Terry, watching the older runners warm up. One of them, a boy in a red singlet, tore out fast in his interval and finished slow, wobbling like the last shopper at a closing store. Oliver turned the pattern over in his mind. Two runners, two races, the same shape: fast first lap, terrible second. Maybe the second lap wasn't the problem at all. Maybe the first lap was quietly doing the damage, the way an anonymous vandal smears a wall and disappears before anyone sees the cause. He couldn't watch the energy drain out of his own legs, but he could see its results.

So he ran a test. First lap, all out: fifty-one seconds, then a second lap so slow Terry had to walk alongside him. Next attempt, he held back deliberately, keeping Sahil's claps as a metronome, and ran two laps that felt almost even. When he checked the watch, the slower-starting version was faster overall by nearly four seconds. The whole race transformed just by changing the beginning.

He practiced the controlled pace Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, while Ms. Addo, the coach who supervised the track after school, marked his splits without comment. Thursday evening she only said, "You're not the same runner you were last week," and clicked her stopwatch.

Friday came grey and cool, the lanes freshly painted white. The field of eight loaded into the staggers, and the gun cracked. The boy in lane five surged immediately, five metres clear by the first bend, and Oliver let him go. It felt wrong, like standing still while a carnivore closed in, but he counted his rhythm and held it. Down the back straight of the second lap, the early leader began to shorten his stride. Oliver passed him on the bend, then Terry's brother, then one more runner drifting backwards like a boat losing its engine. He crossed the line second overall, legs burning but still turning over, and bent double gasping at the infield grass.

Sahil jogged over with the watch and crouched beside him. "Two seconds faster than your old best."

Oliver looked up at the scoreboard, at his lane number still glowing there. "Same legs," he said. "Different first lap."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: In tropical rainforests, the difference between day and night temperatures can be larger than the difference between the warmest and coolest months.
story:
Louis skidded across the polished airport floor and dropped into the plastic chair beside Hayden, who was holding two crumpled sheets of printed graphs like they were treasure maps. "You brought them," Louis panted. "Rainfall and temperature, desert versus rainforest. Best homework ever."

"Mr. Traoré said we had to compare them before the flight," Hayden said, smoothing the pages on his knees. "My mom's taking us to the botanical garden the day we land, the big glass rainforest dome." Their gate announcement flickered overhead, and sunlight refracted through the huge windows onto the graphs, making the little bars glow.

Louis grabbed the temperature sheet. The desert line plunged and soared across the months, twenty degrees of difference between the hottest and coolest. The rainforest line was nearly flat, warm all year. "Easy," he said. "Desert swings, rainforest doesn't. I'd pack shorts for the rainforest and be done." He zipped his backpack triumphantly.

Then his phone buzzed. A message from Aurelia, who was already at her grandmother's village near real rainforest: "Guess what? Days are HOT but nights are COLD here. My grandma made me wear a sweater after dinner. A sweater! In the tropics! Check the daily range, not just monthly." Louis read it twice, frowning. "That can't be right," he told Hayden. "Look, the whole year barely changes."

"The months, yeah," Hayden said slowly. "But she said day and night."

Louis pulled out his pencil and turned the sheet over, sketching a quick test: two little temperature curves, one for a rainforest day. Day up, night down. If nights dropped that far, then the jump between afternoon and midnight could be bigger than the whole spread from the warmest month to the coolest. He stared at his sketch, then laughed out loud. "She's right. The day-night difference can beat the monthly one. I would have frozen."

"You almost did," Hayden said, grinning. "Ready to freeze in a dome?"

Louis unzipped his backpack, pulled out his extra shirt, and stuffed a sweater in beside the graphs, next to the nutritious trail mix his dad had packed and the brochure about rainforest agriculture he'd promised Aurelia he'd read. He patted the bag once. "Sweater for the tropics," he announced. "Aurelia gets the first apology text in history."

"Second," Hayden said, boarding pass in hand. "You'll be apologizing all week."

Louis stood up, shouldered the bag, and said, "Then let's go find out how cold midnight feels under the trees."

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Chlorine bleach must never be mixed with cleaners containing ammonia, because together they release chloramine, a toxic gas.
story:
Florence had exactly forty minutes before the 4:15 bus, because her mother's work shirt had to be clean and folded by the time she got home, and the shirt was currently smudged with mustard from lunch. She had offered to do the laundry herself, mostly to prove she could, and now she was standing in the laundry room with her friend Louise, who had come along "for supervision" and was eating crackers on the dryer.

"Sort first," Florence said, reading the crumpled instruction sheet her mom had left. "Darks with darks, lights with lights." She made two piles on the floor, dropped her blue hoodie with the darks, and put the white work shirt in a basket by itself. The mustard stain sat on the pocket like a small yellow flag. Louise leaned over and said her grandmother used something called bleach on stains like that, which sent Florence digging under the sink, where she found a bottle of chlorine bleach and a spray bottle of something labelled "ammonia-based cleaner."

She set the two bottles side by side on the machine and planned it out like a math problem. Bleach for the shirt, the spray for the sink, both before the bus came. She had to budget her minutes: five for spraying, twenty-five for washing, ten for drying and folding. But as she turned the bleach bottle to read the back, her stomach tightened. The label said never mix with ammonia cleaners. The spray bottle's label, when she checked it, said the same thing in the opposite direction.

"What does that even mean, mix?" Louise asked, hopping off the dryer. "You'd just use one and then the other."

Florence stared at the two bottles. Her dad fixed cars, and he called problems like this a variable, something you changed to see what changed after it. She had learned the hard way, with a ruined sweater, that some things in laundry were volatile, that a small wrong move made a big mess. But this didn't feel like a ruined sweater. This felt like a warning written in capital letters for a reason she couldn't see. She thought about pouring a little of each into the sink drain, just to test whether anything happened, and then she thought about the labels again. "Never mix." She put the caps back on both bottles, tight.

"We're not testing that one," she said. "The label says mixing chlorine bleach and ammonia cleaners makes a toxic gas. Chloramine, it's called." She carried the ammonia spray out to the garage shelf, came back, and treated the stain with bleach alone, exactly as the shirt's tag instructed. The washer hummed. At 4:10 she pulled the warm shirt from the dryer, folded the sleeves the way her mom did, and set it on top of the machine like evidence. From the driveway, they heard the bus turn the corner. "Next time," Louise said, grabbing her backpack, "you're teaching me the sorting part."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Hostile attribution bias is the tendency to assume someone meant to hurt you when what they did was unclear or could easily have been an accident.
story:
Rebecca climbed the bus steps holding her ballot for the spirit week vote crumpled in her fist, and the first thing she saw was June sitting three rows up next to Millie, laughing about something, in the exact seat where Rebecca always sat. June didn't even look back. Rebecca compressed herself into an empty seat near the back and stared at the back of June's head. She had texted June twice last night about saving seats, and June had answered neither one. So it wasn't an accident. It was a message.

"You okay back there?" Mr. Li called into his mirror before he pulled the door shut. "Seatbelt's twisted, fix it before we roll."

Rebecca yanked the strap flat. Millie turned around, saw her face, and twisted back around fast, which Rebecca also decided to add to the evidence. By the time the bus stopped at the light by the bakery, she had the whole case built: June wanted to sit with Millie instead, June was ditching her, and the unanswered texts proved it. The worst part was that they were supposed to count the ballots together at lunch, like they did every year. Rebecca decided she would count them alone.

At the next stop, Millie actually got up and walked back, holding the rail against the sway of the bus. She dropped into the seat across the aisle.

"June's phone died last night," Millie said. "Dead dead, she left her charger at her grandma's. She kept trying to get it to turn on this morning. And she saved your seat, but then Marcus tripped carrying his trombone case and knocked your backpack into the aisle and some kid sat on the seat, and June couldn't exactly throw him off the bus."

Rebecca looked at the three-rows-up seat again. June's shoulders were hunched now, and she was glancing toward the back every few seconds the way you do when you're waiting to find out if you're in trouble. Rebecca realized she had read every single thing wrong, and it had happened because when she didn't know why something happened, she had picked the meanest possible reason and treated it like a fact.

"My brother calls that hostile attribution bias," Millie said. "Assuming somebody meant to hurt you when it could just as easily have been an accident."

"Your brother needs to stop reading his psych homework out loud," Rebecca said, but she was already moving up the aisle, one hand on the seats, past Marcus and his endangered trombone case, which the driver was forever warning would be the death of somebody.
