She slid into the seat across from June.

"Your phone died," Rebecca said.

"My phone died." June held up the dark screen like proof. "I thought you were ignoring me because I ignored you, which I didn't."

"Okay," Rebecca said. "Ballots at lunch?"

"Ballots at lunch," June said, and stuck out her pinky.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Many U.S. schools require a sports physical, a checkup by a doctor or other clinician, before a student is allowed to try out or practice with a team.
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and sweat before anyone had even sweated, and Ariana wondered if gyms always smelled like the future of tryouts. Ms. Bighorn stood at the door of the gymnasium with a clipboard, and every seventh grader had to say their name before walking through. Ariana noticed that some kids walked in and some kids walked right back out, holding a slip of paper, and she wanted to know why. It wasn't random. She counted. Nine went in, three came out, seven went in, two came out.

"You need a sports physical," Mehar reported when she came back from the door, holding her slip. "A checkup by a doctor or other clinician. That's what the paper says. The signed form has to be in before you can try out or even practice with the team." Mehar's shoulders drooped. "I had my checkup last week. I just forgot the form at home on the counter."

"So it's not that the coach doesn't want you," Ariana said slowly, working it out. "It's a rule. A checkup by a doctor or other clinician, before you're allowed to try out or practice. Every school does it." She looked down the line at the kids still waiting, and a pattern was forming in her head like a constellation. "The kids going back out are the ones who don't have the form. The rule doesn't care how good you are. It only cares about the paper."

"My mom's at work until six," Mehar said. "Tryouts end at five."

Ariana borrowed a pencil from Ms. Bighorn and wrote a message on the back of Mehar's slip, printing the school address in careful block letters. "Text your mom this. Tell her to photograph the signed physical form and email it to the office, or take a picture of the picture, or drive here, or send it by carrier pigeon. Anything. Then run home and get the original if you have to. I'll save you a spot in line." Mehar's thumbs flew over her phone, and Ariana watched her run out through the double doors like the gym was on fire.

The tryout itself was drills first, then scrimmaging. Ariana was fast but her left hand was clumsy, so she made herself dribble only with her left through the whole cone line, missing twice, then not missing. A parliament of eighth graders, the Owls varsity, sat in the bleachers watching, and someone had once told her that a group of owls was called a parliament, which seemed right, because they sat there judging like a tiny government. When Ariana banked in a layup she shouldn't have attempted, one of the Owls nodded, just once, and Ariana felt taller.

At the end, Ms. Bighorn read names for the second day of tryouts. "Ariana. Joshua." Then, "Mehar, pending form, and it just came through, so, Mehar." The team burst into applause so sudden and complete it was unanimous, even the kids who hadn't made it clapping, and Mehar came running back in with the paper held over her head like a trophy. She skidded to a stop beside Ariana, breathless.

"You didn't accuse me of being a bad teammate when I got sent out," she panted. "You just fixed it."

"The rule was the problem, not you," Ariana said. Then Ms. Bighorn asked for everyone's form one more time, just to double-check her clipboard, and Ariana reached into her backpack and found only a granola bar, a bent pencil, and her empty folder where the signed physical was supposed to be. She looked at the clipboard. She looked at the clock.

"Ms. Bighorn?" she said. "Does a photograph of the form count if my dad emails it in the next ten minutes?"

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The United States Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on it and farmed it for five years.
story:
Lea spread the photocopied pages of a settler's diary across the kitchen table and glared at them. Her assignment was to use one primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s, but the diary's writer, a woman named Hannah Cole, spent half her ink on weather. "Rain again," one entry said. "The beans did not pollinate, and I fear the bees have gone." Another complained about a wagon that lost part of its cargo crossing a muddy river. Nowhere did Hannah simply announce her reason for leaving Ohio.

On the video call, Martha leaned so close to her camera that Lea could count her freckles. "I found something at my grandpa's house," Martha said, holding up a stiff old paper so fast it blurred. "Hold still," Lea said. When Martha steadied it, Lea read the printed words at the top: it was a land claim, dated 1864, and it mentioned 160 acres of public land, granted under a law that let settlers have it if they lived on the land and farmed it for five years. "Grandpa says it's how our family got the farm," Martha said. "I want to frame it for his birthday, but first I want to know what it actually means, because he keeps saying our whole story started with that paper."

Lea remembered something then. Last autumn, before the unit started, Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya had passed around a ledger page from a ship's cargo and asked them what a receipt could prove about a journey nobody alive had seen. "A document shows you a choice somebody made," he had said, "and choices have reasons hiding under them." So Lea went back to Hannah's diary with a pencil and tried an experiment. She underlined every entry where Hannah mentioned land, then counted the years between Hannah's arrival on her claim and the entry where she wrote, "Today the land is ours by law."

Five years, exactly. Lea flipped to the front and found Hannah's departure date from Ohio, 1863, after the law of 1862. "Martha," she said, holding the diary pages up to her screen, "your paper says 160 acres of public land for settlers who lived on it and farmed it five years. Hannah's diary says she left right after that law, and she counts off five years on her claim. That's why she went west. It was never the weather." Martha whooped so loudly that Lea's cat bolted off the table.

Later, Lea taped one diary page beside her draft and wrote her opening sentence. It felt good, but not as good as what came after, when Martha texted a photo of the framed land paper propped on her grandpa's cake. Lea grinned and typed back, "Tell him happy birthday from Hannah Cole."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In the Sally-Anne test, first used in 1985, children from about age four usually say a character will look where she left her marble, not where it was moved while she was away.
story:
"Forty minutes until we cut the cake," Clara's mother called from the kitchen, and Clara had until then to prove her point.

Her little cousin, four years old and sticky from the fruit punch, sat on the rug in the den. Clara had put a marble in a small basket and told him she was going to hide it. "Remember, it's in the basket," she said. He nodded. Then she sent him to the kitchen with Enoch to help carry napkins, and while he was gone she moved the marble into the red box on the shelf.

"You're wasting your cake time," said Braelyn from the doorway. Braelyn was twelve and treated every one of Clara's ideas with the same flat skepticism. "He'll just look in the box. He saw you touch it."

"He didn't see anything. He was in the kitchen." Clara set both containers side by side on the rug. "That's the whole point."

Enoch came back with the cousin and a stack of napkins. "Mr. Sinclair told me to bring these in before the cake," he said, dropping them on the couch. "He says we've got half an hour now, so hurry up."

Clara knelt in front of her cousin. "Where will you look for the marble?"

The boy pointed at the basket. "In there."

"But it's not in there anymore," Enoch said.

Clara shot him a look. "Don't tell him." She waited until her cousin stopped chewing on his sleeve. "Show us. Go find the marble."

He lifted the basket lid, patted the empty bottom, and frowned. Then he checked under the rug, then behind the box. Only when he tipped the red box and the marble rolled out did he grin and hold it up.

"Beginner's luck," Braelyn said. "Ask him where he thought it was."

"Where did you look first?" Clara asked.

"The basket," the boy said, and wandered off toward the punch bowl, indifferent to the three older kids staring at him.

Clara stood up. "That's exactly it. He looked in the basket because that's where he left it, even though it wasn't there anymore. In my psych book it's called the Sally-Anne test, from 1985. Kids from about age four mostly say the character will look where she left her marble, not where somebody moved it while she was away." She counted on her fingers. "He's four, and he did it, and I predicted it before he moved."

Braelyn folded her arms. "You predicted he'd be wrong."

"I predicted what he'd do. Wrong had nothing to do with it."

From the kitchen her mother's voice rose over the noise. "Twenty minutes! Where's the cake knife?"

Enoch was already herding the cousin toward the kitchen, one hand on his shoulder, the napkins forgotten on the couch. Clara grabbed the marble and the basket and followed, and Braelyn, after a moment, picked up the red box too.

"If he asks for the marble at the table," Braelyn said, "I'm telling him you moved it."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms became part of Canada's Constitution when it was proclaimed on April 17, 1982.
story:
Jordan's class had a civics assignment due Monday: pick one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and explain it in his own words. He had put it off all weekend, and now his mom was working at the polling station downtown, so he rode along with his notebook and a pencil.

The gym smelled like floor wax and coffee. Ms. Doyle, the returning officer, had pinned a Charter poster beside the voter list, tall as a door. Jordan stood in front of it while his mom checked people in behind him. Section 2 listed fundamental freedoms: conscience, religion, thought, belief, opinion, expression. Section 3 gave every citizen the right to vote. He copied section 3 into his notebook, then noticed the date printed along the bottom edge. "Proclaimed April 17, 1982," he read aloud.

Griffin was there too, handing out pencils near the ballot boxes because his older sister was a poll clerk. "Why does the year matter?" he asked.

"Because my grandpa voted before 1982," Jordan said. "If the Charter became part of the Constitution when it was proclaimed on April 17, 1982, then it wasn't part of the Constitution before that. So the right to vote in section 3 couldn't have come from the Charter back then." He wanted to test this, so he wrote a note on a scrap of paper and gave it to Griffin to deliver to his sister at the far table. The message read: "Ask Mom if Grandpa voted before 1982 and what law let him. Send answer back."

Griffin carried it over, waited, and came back with a reply in looping handwriting. "Yes, 1974, federal election. There was an older law, the Canada Elections Act. Grandpa still has his voter card somewhere."

"So voting existed before the Charter," Jordan said. "The Charter didn't create it. It protects it. That's the difference." He crossed out his first draft, which had said the Charter gave Canadians the vote, and started over. "Section 3 means the government can't restrict who gets to vote based on things it shouldn't, like what you think or where your family came from. If a law tries to, the Charter stands in the way."

Griffin leaned over his shoulder. "You should also do a critique of your first draft. You wrote 'gives' twice."

"It was wrong, that's all." Jordan kept writing. Ms. Doyle passed by with a stack of ballots and glanced at the poster.

"Is it feasible to finish that here before we close?" she asked.

"Yes. Ten minutes." Jordan read his new paragraph once through, underlined section 3, and showed it to Griffin. "Say it back to me. If you can explain it, I did it right."

Griffin squinted at the page. "Every citizen gets to vote, and the Charter keeps the government from taking that away."

Jordan closed the notebook. "Exactly. Now I just need Grandpa's voter card for show and tell."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Dutch army surgeon Antonius Mathijsen developed the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones and published his method in 1852.
story:
Lillian sat on the gurney with her left arm cradled against her chest, breathing the way the nurse had shown her: in through the nose, out through the mouth. The wrist had gone purple and puffy, and every bump of the wheels on the tile floor sent a hot wire of pain up to her elbow. Roxanne, who had ridden in the ambulance with her because Lillian's mom was stuck in traffic, kept hold of her good hand the whole way.

"It was the ramp," Roxanne said. "The skate park ramp has that crack near the bottom. It's getting worse."

"That's what I thought too," Lillian said. "But watch." She pointed at Roxanne's phone, which showed a slow-motion video Arnaud had taken before anyone dialed 911. "My wheels aren't near the crack. I landed with all my weight on the board at a bad angle. The ramp didn't do it. I did it." She hated knowing that, but knowing was better than blaming a crack that other kids would keep skating over.

The doctor came back with a cart of little tubs, each one a different color. "Time to pick your cast," she said. Roxanne immediately chose tropical orange, but Lillian paused. "Before there were casts," she asked, "what did people do? Just... lie still forever?"

The doctor laughed and pulled up something on the tablet mounted by the bed. "Look this up yourself if you want, but here's the short version. A Dutch army surgeon named Antonius Mathijsen developed the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones, and he published his method in 1852." She turned the screen so Lillian could see the old drawing, soldiers' legs wrapped stiff and pale. Lillian read it twice, mouthing the year. Plaster of Paris. So casts weren't some brand-new invention; they were older than cars, older than light bulbs, and they still worked the same basic way, wet wrapping that hardened around a broken bone.

"Blue," she said. "Blue like the ocean."

While the doctor wrapped layer after layer, Arnaud arrived, out of breath, carrying Lillian's backpack and a slushie. "I figured you'd want your sketchbook," he said. "I got you blue raspberry, but, um, don't slurp too fast or you'll jostle."

"That's the plan," Lillian said. "The slushie is now a slow ritual. One sip every five minutes, left hand stays perfectly still." Roxanne counted the first five minutes on her watch, then held the straw while Lillian drank, careful as someone defusing a bomb.

Lillian flexed the fingers poking out of the blue cast. "Six weeks of this," she said. Roxanne raised her slushie like a toast. "Six weeks of us signing it, starting now."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A percentage based on very few attempts can be misleading: a player who makes one shot out of one attempt shoots 100 percent.
story:
Alexis slid into the red booth between her dad and her older brother, breathing in the smell of nachos and buffalo sauce. Above the bar, three screens glowed with basketball stats, and the whole place hummed with shouting and laughing. Then she spotted Taya two tables over, waving wildly.

"You're here!" Taya squeezed through the crowd and leaned over the booth. "Guess what. I checked the league site this morning. My shooting percentage is one hundred percent."

"One hundred?" Alexis's brother snorted into his soda.

"Perfect," Taya said, buoyant as a beach ball. "Every shot I took went in."

Alexis felt a flicker of doubt, small but sharp, like a pebble in her sneaker. Taya had barely played this season. "How many shots did you take?"

Taya counted on her fingers, then held up one. "One. Coach put me in for the last minute of the Marshall game, and I made the layup."

"One out of one," Alexis said slowly. She grabbed a napkin and borrowed her brother's pen. In wobbly letters she wrote it out: one made, one attempted, one hundred percent. Then, underneath, she wrote Violette's numbers from the same site, which she remembered because Violette never stopped talking about them: forty-two made out of eighty attempts. She did the division twice on the napkin's corner. Violette's percentage came out to about fifty-three percent.

"So on paper," Alexis said, "your number is better than Violette's. But it's just one shot." She looked up at the big screen, where a scroll of player stats marched past. "All these numbers are like that. They squash a whole season into one figure."

Taya frowned at the napkin. "So my one hundred percent doesn't really mean anything?"

"It means you haven't missed yet," Alexis said. "That's all it can tell anyone." She could infer the rest without saying it: Violette had proven herself over eighty chances, and Taya had proven nothing except one lucky, perfect layup.

Taya's grin came back, defiant. "Then I need more shots. Tomorrow at practice I'm taking fifty." She jabbed a finger at the napkin. "Keep that. I want to see my percentage after."

Alexis folded it into her jacket pocket just as the nachos arrived, steaming and piled high. Taya snatched a chip, pointed it at the glowing screen like a sword, and said, "See you at fifty attempts."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the atomic number also tells you how many electrons it has.
story:
Owen had never noticed the framed poster in Grandpa's study before, but on Saturday afternoon it was the only thing on the wall that mattered. It was a periodic table, faded at the corners, with tiny numbers tucked above each symbol. His science test was Monday, and his own textbook was sitting on the kitchen counter at home, forty minutes away. His mom had said the trip to Grandpa's was temporary, just one weekend, but a test didn't care where your book was.

He copied elements onto a napkin until his pen ran dry, then went looking for a pencil. Instead he found Grandpa in the kitchen holding Owen's phone, which had been buzzing like a trapped wasp. "Your friend Siena has texted you nine times," Grandpa said.

Owen took the phone. Siena was building a model of a sodium atom for the same test, out of a foam ball and pushpins, and she was stuck. "How many electrons do I put on it?" her latest message read. "The sheet just says sodium has atomic number 11. I looked everywhere and it only says protons. I'm going to glue the pins on wrong."

Owen stared at the poster in the study. Eleven protons, sure, that part was easy. But electrons were the mystery. You couldn't see them, couldn't count them, and the poster didn't list them anywhere. He tried to assess the problem like a coach would: what did he actually know? A neutral atom had no charge. An atom with no charge couldn't have extra of anything, or it would be lopsided. If protons and electrons weren't balanced, the whole thing would be off balance. So in a neutral atom, the number of electrons had to equal the number of protons. He sat back. That meant the atomic number told you both.

He texted Siena: "11 electrons. Atomic number counts protons, and in a neutral atom electrons equal protons, so it gives you electrons too." Then he tested it against the poster, hunting through elements to see if the pattern ever broke his rule. Neon, atomic number 10. Ten protons, ten electrons. Carbon, six and six. His hand was shaking a little as he worked, the way it did when a puzzle snapped together.

Then Grandpa appeared in the doorway with two mugs. "That poster," he said, "I hung it when I taught chemistry. Forty years."

Owen gaped at him. Grandpa had always been the grandpa who canned tomatoes and fell asleep during baseball games. Owen realized he'd been working from a stereotype of what an old man in a cardigan knew. "Why didn't you say anything?"

"You didn't ask," Grandpa said. "And you didn't need me. Siena's model will have eleven pins, and you found that out yourself." He set a mug beside the napkin covered in numbers. "Check the bottom right corner of the poster sometime. Element 118."

Owen leaned close. The space was blank except for a penciled note in his grandfather's handwriting: "Still counting."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Viola Spolin's 1963 book 'Improvisation for the Theater' collected theater games and is often called the bible of improv teaching.
story:
Riley stood on the small stage of the community theatre, holding a plastic teacup, while Mr. Kelly wrote "Scene: astronauts on a sinking ship" on the whiteboard. Riley wanted the camp's Friday showcase slot more than anything, but every time he improvised with Elaine, he froze, because once, in last year's talent show, he had planned a whole skit with jokes he'd written at home, and when the audience didn't laugh at the first one, he forgot the rest and just stood there until his cousin pulled him offstage. Planning had failed him, so now he needed to learn the opposite thing.

"Whatever your partner gives you, take it and add to it," Mr. Kelly said. "That's the whole game." He held up a battered paperback with a cracked spine. "Viola Spolin wrote this in 1963. It collects theater games, and people call it the bible of improv teaching." He set it on the edge of the stage and clapped his hands.

Elaine started their scene. "Captain, the hold is flooding and the ship is hibernating for the winter." Riley's instinct was to correct her, because spaceships obviously couldn't hibernate, and he almost said so. But correcting felt like the same trap as scripting, blocking whatever came at him. Instead he tested the opposite. "Yes, and the crew will have to sleep in space suits until spring," he said, "or our hereditary fear of water will wake us up."

"That makes no sense," whispered Roman, who was waiting for the next turn with his arms crossed. "You can't inherit a fear of water."

"Watch," Riley said, and turned back to Elaine. She was pouring imaginary tea with the plastic teacup. "Yes, and this tea will keep the ship drowsy," she said, "but Captain, you have to drink it before the seal leaks." Riley drank the tea, hiccupped a bubble, and floated slowly to the floor as if he weighed nothing at all. Roman laughed for real, not the polite kind.

Afterward, Riley sat on the stage edge and picked up the worn book. He turned pages of games with names and diagrams, games other kids had played since before he was born, and understood that the thing that had saved his scene wasn't luck. There was a rule underneath it, invisible until you tried it, and the rule worked both ways, like a door that swings open and shut. When you blocked, everything stopped. When you took the offer and stacked something on top, the scene kept going whether you were funny or not, and that was the part he'd never believed.

At the showcase, Mr. Kelly called their names. Elaine grabbed the plastic teacup and whispered, "Ready, Captain?"

Riley saluted. "Yes, and the winter is coming early this year."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it.
story:
Jordan posted the photo at 8:42 on Friday night, from the lobby of Siege Harbor, where his squad was waiting for the season tournament to open. It showed him mid-rage, headset half off his head, mouth open, after Asher had stolen his loot for the third time. His location tag was on, the way it always was, so the post read "Oaks Recreation Center, Room 3B" right under his face.

He deleted it ten minutes later, once he'd cooled down and remembered that half his classmates followed his account. Gone. He checked twice, scrolling his own page with his thumb while the lobby music looped and Ireland's voice crackled through his headset asking if he was ready. The photo had retired to nowhere. He queued up and forgot about it.

Saturday morning his phone buzzed against the cereal bowl. Asher had dropped the exact photo into the squad group chat, with a caption: "History cannot be erased." Jordan stared at it, the same open mouth, the same rec center address underneath.

He called Ireland. "How? I deleted that."

"Screenshots," Ireland said. "Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it."

Jordan sat back. He remembered Friday night now, the little flash of Asher's screen in the corner of the video call, the click he'd assumed was a game sound. He opened the chat and counted: Asher had sent it, then two classmates he didn't even know followed his account had shared it onward. Strangers. People whose names he'd never seen, passing around his face and the address of the room where he played every Friday.

He typed a message to Asher: "Delete it."

"Can't," Asher sent back. "Already saved by like six people."

Jordan did the only test he could think of. He posted a new photo, a boring one of his sneakers, location tag still on, and waited. Three minutes later a kid named frostbyte99, whom he'd never met, commented "nice shoes oaks rec center kid." Jordan deleted the post, then messaged frostbyte99: "What photo?" The reply came in seconds: "the sneaker one, saved it, why?"

So that was the rule. He went into his settings and switched off location tagging, then scrolled back through months of posts, checking each one for the address of his school, his street, the rec center. His thumb ached by the time he finished. He untagged, deleted, and closed his account settings.

In the lobby that night, the tournament bracket loaded. Ireland's voice came through: "You ready?"

Jordan pulled on his headset. "Born ready," he said, and hit accept.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Sikh gurdwaras serve langar, a free communal meal offered to every visitor regardless of religion, often with everyone seated together on the floor.
story:
Lillian had told Iman three times that she didn't need to bring money, but Iman kept patting her jacket pocket anyway, as if the five dollars might fall out and get lost in the parking lot. The gurdwara smelled of warm dough and cardamom, and the hallway was humid from all the cooking. Through a doorway Lillian could see rows and rows of people sitting cross-legged on the floor, shoulder to shoulder.

"How much is the meal?" Iman whispered, craning her neck.

"There's no charge," Lillian said. "It's called langar."

"Free? For anybody?"

"Every visitor," Lillian said. "Doesn't matter who you are or what religion." She watched Iman do the math in her head, glancing at the strangers, the aunties in bright suits, the man in a Jets hoodie, two little kids squabbling over a spot near the fan. Iman was clearly waiting for the catch. Lillian knew that look, because for years she'd had it too, until her grandmother pointed out that she kept looking for a cash box that didn't exist.

They found a stretch of carpet near the back and sat down. Volunteers moved down the rows with steel buckets, and a woman ladled dal onto Lillian's steel tray, then Iman's, without pausing or asking anything. Iman held her tray stiffly, still in suspense, still waiting for someone to tap her shoulder and say there had been a mistake. When the roti came around, folded in a cloth napkin, she took one and whispered, "This is really good."

Afterward, Iman followed Lillian to the sink to wash hands, but she didn't leave the kitchen doorway. Inside, a man was rolling dough into perfect circles while a woman worked the hot tawa with a long metal turner. A boy about their age, Royce from their science class, stood at a counter stacking roti into cloth bundles, and Lillian hadn't even known he was Sikh.

"Can I help?" Iman asked, so suddenly that Royce looked up.

"There's an empty spot," he said, scooting over. "Just keep them coming to the left side."

Lillian watched Iman take up the stack of warm roti and carry it out to the rows, kneeling beside strangers and offering bread with both hands, the way she'd seen the volunteers do it. When two little kids started arguing over who got to sit closest to the fan, Iman stepped between them and mediated, suggesting they take turns, and somehow they actually listened.

Later, in the parking lot, Iman pulled the five dollars out of her pocket and stared at it. "I didn't need this at all."

"You can keep it for the book fair," Lillian said.

Iman laughed and put it back. "Next time I'm bringing an appetite instead."

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: To change a speed in meters per second into kilometers per hour, multiply it by 3.6.
story:
Louis crouched at the top of the skate park's biggest ramp with a tennis ball in one hand and his phone in the other, and Laurence stood at the bottom holding a broom handle they had found behind the bins. "When I drop it, start counting seconds," Louis said. "Not with the phone. The phone stopwatch makes you impulsive, you tap it too early." Laurence looked offended but raised the broom anyway, because Laurence was the fastest counter in their class and everyone knew it.

The plan had started that morning in Mr. Pérez's room, where a worksheet about distance-time graphs had seemed like the most boring thing ever invented. Speed equals distance divided by time; draw a line; the steeper the line, the faster the thing. Louis had nearly submerge... no, he had nearly fallen asleep, except Mr. Pérez had said one strange thing on his way past their desk. "A speed in meters per second, times 3.6, gives you kilometers per hour." He had not explained it. He had just kept walking, like he had dropped a coin on the table and left it there.

Now Louis wanted the coin. Vaughn arrived on his bike, skidded to a stop, and asked what they were doing. "Science," said Louis. "We roll the ball, we time it, we find its speed, and then we find out if it beats a person walking." Vaughn frowned. "A person walks about five kilometers an hour, my gran says, she counts everything." He marked a line in the dust with his heel. "So that's the competition. Ball versus gran."

They rolled the ball three times. The ramp to the broom was nine meters; Laurence counted "one-Mississippi" style and got four seconds, then three and a half, then four again. Nine divided by four was 2.25, and Louis did the math twice on the back of his hand because he did not trust his own brain under pressure. Then he remembered the coin. 2.25 times 3.6. He got 8.1. He checked it again. Still 8.1.

"Eight point one kilometers an hour," he announced. Vaughn whooped so loudly that a toddler on a scooter near the bowl turned to stare, and the toddler's dad laughed. "That's faster than your gran!" Vaughn shouted. "Way faster than walking!" Laurence, who was quietly pleased about his counting, said, "So to turn a speed in meters per second into kilometers per hour, you multiply it by 3.6," just to hear it out loud, and Louis grinned because hearing it made it real.

That evening Louis drew the graph in his notebook, one dot for each roll, the line rising like the ramp itself, and his analysis said the ball was not perfectly steady because his dots wobbled a little. He would tell Mr. Pérez tomorrow. He slipped the notebook under his pillow, then took it out again to look at the dots one more time. "Eight point one," he whispered to the ceiling. "Gran, you never stood a chance."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks do not count as at-bats, so the number gives a batter no credit for walks.
story:
Matthew had one goal before dinner: prove that Aris was wrong on the class forum. Aris had posted a chart of batting averages and declared that his favorite player, Rico Vance, didn't belong in the top ten because his average was only .261. Matthew's favorite, Vance's teammate Jordy Okafor, sat at .288, and Matthew intended to end the argument for good.

He settled in at the computer and pulled up the stats page, leaning close to scrutinize every column. Hits. At-bats. Average. Then a fourth column he usually skipped: walks. Vance had 84 of them. Okafor had 31. Matthew frowned. Both players had played the same number of games, yet their at-bats were strangely different. Vance had far fewer. He scrolled, read, and scrolled again, and somewhere in a comment thread below the table he found a kid arguing exactly the opposite of Aris. "Vance is underrated," the kid wrote. "A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks don't count as at-bats, so the number gives a batter no credit for walks."

Matthew read the sentence three times. He grabbed a pencil and tried it himself, dividing Vance's hits by his at-bats on scrap paper. The answer matched the .261 on the screen, which meant the comment was describing something real. Vance reached base constantly, but almost a hundred trips to first base had simply vanished from the number everyone quoted. His instinct told him to defend Okafor anyway, because Okafor was his guy, but the numbers were the numbers.

He typed a reply to Aris and then paused, because the phone buzzed. It was Aris himself, calling instead of texting, which he only did when something was wrong. "My grandma's in the hospital," Aris said, voice wobbling. "I can't finish the chart for Mr. Chanthavong by tomorrow. I started it but I'm stuck."

"Send me what you have," Matthew said. "I'm already on that page anyway." He copied Aris's half-finished chart, filled in the missing averages, and while he worked he noticed something that made him sit up straight: the comment defending Vance had been posted by a username, CoachC77, and the profile picture was unmistakable. It was Mr. Chanthavong, their own teacher, arguing about baseball on a stats site at midnight.

Matthew added a final line to the chart, one distinct note at the bottom in bold: "Vance: .261 average, but 84 walks not counted." Then he texted Aris, "Chart's done. Also, wait until you find out who CoachC77 is."

At school the next morning, Mr. Chanthavong collected the charts without a word, but when he reached Matthew's desk he stopped, tapped the bold note, and raised one eyebrow.

"Nice work," Mr. Chanthavong said. "See me after class, Slugger fan."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Studies have found that a night of sleep after practicing a finger-movement sequence can improve performance the next day without any extra practice.
story:
Noah sat at the upright piano in the music classroom after last bell, working through the same eight measures for the fourth day running. The passage required his right hand to jump a fourth and then cross under, and every time he reached the sixth note his fingers tangled. Mr. Okonkwo had told him the piece was versatile enough to work on either piano or the classroom keyboard, but that didn't help. He ground through it forty more times, hit the same wall, and finally closed the lid.

"You look like despair in a hoodie," said Milania, who was stacking chairs near the door. "That crossing part again?"

"Sixth note. Every single time." He pulled his sleeve down over his hand, as if he could insulate his fingers from their own clumsiness. "I'm going to miss the recital cut at this rate."

At home he practiced once more, badly, and went to bed annoyed.

The next morning he got to school early, before anyone else, and set his backpack on a chair. He told himself he would just check whether the passage was as bad as yesterday, no rehearsing, one run-through. He put his hands on the keys, played the eight measures, and got through them clean, all the way to the end, twice in a row. He had done no extra practice since the night before. He sat there staring at his own hands.

He decided to test it instead of just being glad. He picked a different tricky line from another piece, one he had never practiced, and played it badly that afternoon, fumbling the same spots again and again. Then he left it alone, went home, slept, and did not touch a piano. The next morning he came in early again, and the new line went through without a stumble, no extra practice in between. The same thing had happened twice: a night of sleep after practicing the finger movement made his playing better the next day. He wrote both results in the back of his binder, with dates, so he wouldn't talk himself out of it.

When Milania came in, he was playing the original passage at full speed. She stopped stacking chairs.

"When did you fix that?"

"Last night," Noah said. "I was asleep."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Slow breathing with long exhales can calm the body's stress response, which is why it is a common coping skill before a stressful moment.
story:
The group chat pinged at 6:47, and Jayden read the first message twice before it made sense. Uriah had written, "It's happening Saturday. Coach picked three of us to take penalty shots in front of everyone at the end of practice." Jayden's thumbs hovered. He knew exactly what Uriah meant, because Jayden was one of the three. He hadn't told anyone yet, not even Michelle, and the anxiety had been sitting in his stomach like a stone since Tuesday, when the coach read out the names and the whole team turned to look.

"You okay?" Michelle typed. "You've been weird in here all week. Like, you start messages and delete them. I can see 'Uriah is typing' happen."

"It's nothing," Jayden sent, then felt bad about it, because it wasn't nothing and Michelle could tell. She'd been trying to organize the science fair group all week, and Jayden kept dodging her, and at some point a friend had a legitimate right to know why. He took a breath and typed the truth. "I'm one of the three taking penalties. Saturday. In front of everybody."

"Wait," Michelle replied. "That's why your messages migrate from topic to topic every time practice comes up. You're steering away from it."

Before Jayden could answer, Uriah sent a photo of a folded note from the goalie, slipped into his locker after practice. The note said: "You looked stressed before tryouts last year and it wrecked your touch. Here's what I do before a penalty shot. I breathe slow and make the exhale longer than the inhale. Slow breathing with long exhales is how I cope before a stressful moment. It settles the body down. Try it before Saturday." Uriah added, "Is this real or is he messing with me? It sounds made up."

Jayden stared at the note. It sounded made up. But he thought about the goalie, about how he never looked rattled, and he decided there was one way to find out. He set a timer on his phone, sat on his bedroom floor, and tried it, in for three, out longer than in, over and over. Nothing magical happened. But his shoulders dropped, and the stone in his stomach got smaller. He did it again Thursday after a rough scrimmage, and again Friday night when he couldn't sleep.

Saturday morning the chat filled up fast. Michelle: "You've got this." Uriah: "Doing the goalie thing in the car. Weirdly works." Then the chat went quiet, because all three of them were walking onto the field.

The coach set the ball down. Jayden took his spot at the arc, and behind him he could hear the whole team shifting on the bench. He didn't look at them. He breathed in, then let the breath out slow, longer than it came in, the way he'd practiced, and the noise seemed to move somewhere behind glass. The keeper rocked on his heels. Jayden pivoted his plant foot and struck the ball.
